title: Thread-Safe LRU Cache
description: Make the LRU cache thread-safe using locks, ConcurrentHashMap, and read-write locks for high-concurrency environments.

segments.text: Our LRU cache works perfectly in a single thread. But in production, dozens of threads hit it simultaneously. Without thread safety, you get corrupted pointers, lost entries, and mysterious crashes. Let's fix that.

The race condition: Thread A calls get on key X and starts moving the node to head. Thread B calls put, which evicts the tail. If X happens to be at the tail, Thread A holds a reference to a node that Thread B just removed. Dangling pointer.
The simplest fix: a global lock. Wrap every get and put call in a synchronized block or ReentrantLock. This guarantees correctness but serializes all access. High contention means poor throughput.

Better: a ReadWriteLock. Multiple threads can read simultaneously since get does not modify the map. Only write operations like put and eviction need exclusive access. Reads are fast, writes are safe.
Wait. Think carefully about that last point.
segments.thought_prompt: Does get really not modify anything? Remember, it moves the accessed node to the head of the list. That IS a write operation!

segments.text: Exactly. In an LRU cache, get is also a write because it updates the access order. So a pure ReadWriteLock does not help much here. We need a different approach for truly concurrent reads.

Java's ConcurrentHashMap uses segment-level locking. Replace HashMap with ConcurrentHashMap for the key-to-node mapping. But the linked list still needs its own synchronization since ConcurrentHashMap does not protect pointer manipulation.
Advanced approach: striped locks. Divide the cache into N shards, each with its own lock, hash map, and linked list. A key's shard is determined by hash modulo N. Contention drops by a factor of N.

Google Guava's Cache uses exactly this pattern. Sixteen segments by default, each independently locked. It also handles expiration, weak references, and statistics. In production, prefer battle-tested libraries over hand-rolled implementations.

In Python, the GIL gives you some safety for simple operations, but not for compound ones. Use threading.Lock around get and put. For async systems, use asyncio locks instead. The cachetools library handles this for you.

segments.thought_prompt: With 16 shards, each shard has capacity/16 entries. What happens when one shard is hot and others are cold?

segments.text: Hot shards evict more aggressively, reducing effective cache size. Solutions include consistent hashing for better distribution or a shared eviction pool. Thread-safe caching is a deep topic. The key lesson: correctness first, then optimize for concurrency.
